item.title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 18 November 2026
item.description:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Key Highlights

  • An Israeli airstrike on Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis area of Gaza killed six people and damaged critical surgical facilities, further undermining efforts to restore the Strip’s severely overstretched health system.
  • As Gaza enters its fourth winter since October 2023, early seasonal rainfall has already caused flooding and damage to thousands of shelters, while humanitarian partners have called for the urgent entry of winter supplies and access to safer locations.
  • Food Security Sector partners highlighted the urgent need to facilitate the entry of veterinary kits into Gaza to protect livestock, preserve herding livelihoods and address parasite infestations that pose risks to human, animal and environmental health, particularly during winter.
  • In Jericho, West Bank, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot and killed by an Israeli settler. Overall, 40 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage were recorded across 30 communities in one week.
  • Settler attacks and related access restrictions displaced 68 Palestinians, including 31 children, in Hebron and Ramallah governorates during the same week. The Jordan Valley has accounted for 44 per cent of Palestinians displaced in this context in 2026.
  • Since the beginning of 2026, more than 5,150 Palestinians have been displaced across the West Bank due to demolitions, settler violence and related access restrictions, and evictions, averaging more than 16 people per day.

item.title: Myanmar Health Cluster Strategy 2027-2028
item.description:
Country: Myanmar
Source: Health Cluster

Please refer to the attached file.

Myanmar has been affected by the devastating impact of natural disasters like earthquakes, floods and cyclones and armed conflict
since the military coup that took place on 1 February 2021.

Access to health care is severely impeded by continuous bombs and drone strikes, killing and maiming health workers, and damaging
and destroying health facilities and infrastructure, aggravated by roadblocks and impassable roads during the rainy season. Between
1 January and 23 November 2026, 142 attacks on health care were reported by Insecurity Insight (https://mapaction-maps.herokuapp.com/health), as compared to 67 verified attacks recorded by WHO’s Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (https://extranet.who.int/ssa/Index.aspx) in the same time period.

Active conflict and natural disasters are resulting in loss of lives and livelihoods, as well as displacement, worsening the already
immense mental health problems in the country. Over 4M people are internally displaced as of 26 October 2026 (https://data.unhcr.org/en/situations/myanmar).

In spite of admirable efforts of health partners that deliver health services under the most challenging of circumstances, the overall
health situation in Myanmar continues to deteriorate. A severe lack of skilled health workers and chronic shortages in life-saving
supplies are compounding the weak health system with 41% of assessed health facilities not able to fully operate.

Almost 15M people out of the 56M population in Myanmar, have been identified as in need of humanitarian aid according to the
2027 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP). Out of these, at least 10.1M people are in need of support with basic health
care, including 2.7M IDPs. Women, children, older people and people with disabilities, and those with mental health needs are
facing heightened risks and barriers to accessing care. Crowded settlements, unsafe drinking water, inadequate sanitation, and the
interruption of routine health programs are posing a serious threat to public health:

  • Cholera cases were detected simultaneously in 4 different parts of the country between May and August 2026, following a
    similar pattern as a large-scale cholera outbreak that spread through Myanmar in 2024,
  • Malaria and dengue are continuing to see an alarming resurgence,
  • Increasing risk of vaccine-preventable diseases like measles and polio, resulting from lack of immunization, leaving over 1.5
    million children under-five without basic vaccinations.
  • Absence of treatment for communicable diseases like TB, HIV and Leprosy in large parts of the country is resulting in
    preventable disability and death, as well as worsening disease outcomes, including resistance to common medicines.

item.title: UNICEF Nigeria Humanitarian Flash Update No. 2 (Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease), 13 November 2026
item.description:
Country: Nigeria
Source: UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

  • Nigeria continues to report one laboratory-confirmed imported Ebola case and no deaths. No new Ebola samples or alerts have been received since 6 November.
  • The index case has been discharged from the hospital in Switzerland.
  • The 42-day countdown for Nigeria to be declared BVD-free will end on 7 December 2026 if no new case occurs.
  • UNICEF supported three training batches for 165 frontline health workers and support personnel and is expanding case management, IPC and WASH readiness in the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja and five high-risk states.
  • UNICEF has mobilized US$414,572.40 in Health, IPC (including PPEs), and WASH supplies.

item.title: Afghanistan: Monthly Market Report Issue 77: October 2026
item.description:
Country: Afghanistan
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS

Markets remain functional, but persistent trade disruptions, elevated commodity prices, rising transportation costs and limited employment opportunities continue to constrain household purchasing power.

MACROECONOMIC AND TRADE DEVELOPMENTS

Economic Growth and Household Welfare

Afghanistan's economy continues to recover, with real GDP projected to grow by 3.0% in 2026. However, rapid population growth, partly driven by returning Afghans, continues to outpace economic gains, limiting improvements in per-capita income which is projected to contract by 3.3 percent in 2026. Weak investment, limited job creation and restrictions on women's economic participation continue to constrain household incomes and economic opportunities.

Trade Routes and Supply Network

One year after the Pakistan border closure, Afghanistan's import networks remain increasingly reliant on alternative routes through Iran and Central Asia. Iranian direct trade and transit routes accounted for 56.6 percent of trade flows, while Central Asian corridors contributed 38.9 percent. Longer routes and higher logistics costs continue to increase import expenses and expose domestic markets to supply-chain risks.

Exchange Rate

The Afghani depreciated marginally by 0.5% in October to an average of AFN 64.9/USD. Nevertheless, it remained 2.4% stronger than a year earlier and 7% above its three-year average, helping moderate imported inflationary pressures despite elevated transportation and trade costs.

Inflation (August 2026)

Headline inflation reached 7.8% year-on-year, its highest level since 2022, while food inflation climbed to 8.9%, approaching double digits. Higher costs of food, housing, healthcare and transportation continue to weigh on household budgets.

Fuel and Logistics Costs

Diesel prices remained high in October at AFN 80.4/litre, standing 3% above last year and 13% above the three-year average, sustaining pressure on transportation and market operating costs.

item.title: oPt: Environmental War Crimes: How Israel’s military assault has turned Gaza into a toxic wasteland, threatening human survival (November 2026)
item.description:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: Oxfam

Please refer to the attached file.

More than 99 per cent of Gaza shows indicators of environmental contamination from Israel’s military assault

Military strikes, fires, destruction of buildings and environmental systems have contaminated air, soil and water throughout Gaza.

Israel's destruction of Gaza through the extensive use of explosive and incendiary weapons has made air, soil and water dangerous to Palestinians now and for decades to come, with indicators of toxic contamination across almost the entirety of the Strip.

New analyses in a report released by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) today, has found that Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination risks across Gaza, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants threatening the environmental life support systems that people in Gaza depend upon for survival.

“Environmental War Crimes: How Israel’s military assault has turned Gaza into a toxic wasteland, threatening human survival” found that the scale and intensity of the Israeli military’s onslaught has affected approximately 78 per cent of Gaza’s land area, with the report’s spatial analysis identifying indicators of potential contamination across more than 99 per cent of the territory; highlighting the scale and near-total geographical spread of pollution risks.

“Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come. The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival,” said Oxfam International Executive Director Amitabh Behar. “This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris. These risks will persist for generations to come, unless clean-up, remediation and recovery actions are prioritised.”

Using satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, including existing research on conflict-related contamination in other contexts, the report finds the evidence already available in Gaza is sufficient to conclude contamination is widespread, severe and consequential, with serious implications for public health and civilian survival. However, restrictions on the entry of testing equipment and technical expertise continue to prevent a full assessment of the scale and extent of contamination.

Spatial analysis of the severity and diversity of contamination indicates that the highest levels of potential contamination are concentrated in Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia, and the Salah al-Din Road, reflecting the combined impact of bombardment, widespread destruction and multiple sources of contamination.

At present, recovery and reconstruction discussions are advancing in the absence of a field-level post conflict environmental assessment (PCEA) of conflict-related contamination, a direct result of Israel’s continued refusal of independent access to Gaza.

Behar said: “It is horrifying to begin to understand the extent of toxic contamination being faced by the population, who can neither escape nor protect themselves properly from the dangers. In an area as small, oppressed and densely populated as Gaza, continuous exposure is inevitable, with people surrounded by waste and sewage, spreading pests and the risk of disease growing. Raw sewage is pouring into the sea and leaking into the ground, while the destruction of Gaza’s sanitation systems leaves people with little protection from the contamination around them.

“The associated health consequences will be severe, with children and pregnant women among those facing the highest risks.”

The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that Israel’s military operations have generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, turning Gaza’s destroyed homes, neighbourhoods and infrastructure into a vast reservoir of potentially hazardous materials.

The report builds a comprehensive picture of Gaza’s contamination, with findings including:

  • Faecal coliforms detected at a rate nearly ten times more than that reported in 2021. Analysis of testing data found faecal coliforms in 19 per cent of the 79 groundwater wells sampled across Gaza in July 2026, compared with 2 per cent of groundwater wells reported as contaminated in 2021.
  • Only 19 per cent of sewage pumping stations remain functional, with just 30 per cent of the wastewater network having some operational capacity. This results in approximately 40,000m³ of raw sewage being pouring into the Mediterranean Sea each day, with a further 15,000m³ per day lost from the wastewater collection system through cesspits and other leakage pathways.
  • Areas around Beit Hanoun, Wadi Gaza and northeast of Khan Younis face heightened risks of long-term soil contamination due to their more clay-rich soils, which are more likely to retain pollutants, threatening the safety of food crops when agricultural production resumes.
  • Gaza City, Jabalia and the North Gaza Governorate face the highest risk of air contamination, as pollutants generated by the intensive bombardment are resuspended as contaminated dust into the air by wind, vehicle movement and debris clearance.
  • High risks of drinking-water contamination in North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir al-Balah, where remaining operational wells and desalination overlap with highly vulnerable groundwater systems and areas of heavy bombardment and debris accumulation; with flooding and sewage overflow further increasing the risk of contamination.
  • People in Gaza are facing growing respiratory health risks from dust and pollution caused by the destruction of buildings and the burning of waste, which can irritate the respiratory system, worsen asthma and cause lung injury. The persistence of hazardous materials in the environment raises concerns about prolonged exposure and lasting respiratory harm, particularly concerning children given their vulnerability and higher relative inhalation rates.

Report author Lama Abdul Samad, a global water and sanitation specialist at Oxfam said: “Fixing Gaza’s environment will be highly challenging because contamination is dispersed across the urban rubble, farmlands, water systems and soils, while unexploded ordnance continues to restrict safe access to most areas. The analysis highlights the urgent need for Israel to grant access for a detailed environmental assessment on the ground to clarify the risks to public health and identify options for urgent harm reduction measures. Restoration is likely to require extensive clearance, monitoring and specialised remediation of affected areas from contaminants like explosive residues, organic pollutants, and heavy metals.”

With international attention increasingly turning to Gaza’s reconstruction, environmental recovery must not be treated as an afterthought but as a vital undertaking in parallel.

“Rebuilding Gaza without simultaneously understanding and addressing the extent of environmental contamination risks creating long-term public health consequences for generations to come,” Behar said. “A comprehensive programme of environmental assessment and remediation must form an integral part of Gaza’s recovery and reconstruction plans.”

Oxfam calls on Israel to end its genocide and siege of Gaza and to allow unrestricted access for aid, environmental assessment and essential equipment. It demands that states halt arms transfers to Israel where they sustain the unlawful occupation of the occupied Palestinian territory, or where they are used to commit serious violations of international law. It calls for the funding of a Palestinian-led assessment, clean-up and safe reconstruction.

Recovery and reconstruction of Gaza must be owned and led by Palestinians themselves. It must be rights-based, reparations-oriented, and rooted in accountability. International funding does not replace Israel’s obligation to make reparations for the harm caused by its unlawful acts.

Ends

Contact information

For more information and interviews, please contact:

Jacqui Corcoran, jacqui.corcoran@oxfam.org, +353 872932271

Lisa Rutherford, lisa.rutherford@oxfam.org, +44 (0)7345 772278

Roslyn Boatman, roslyn.boatman@oxfam.org, +961 791 78540

Notes to editors

By November 2026, Israeli forces have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000, while thousands still remainunaccounted for under the rubble.

In early 2026, the United Nations (UN) reported that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives had been dropped on Gaza in almost two years, describing the volume of ordnance deployed as unprecedented and estimating its total energy as equivalent to approximately 13 Hiroshima-sized nuclear bombs.

UNHRC. (26 February 2026). Domicide: Mass Destruction of Housing and Civilian Infrastructure in Gaza, Myanmar, Sudan and Ukraine (A/HRC/61/43/Add.3)

19 per cent of sewage pumping stations remain functional, with just 30 per cent of the wastewater network having some operational capacity resulting in raw sewage being pouring into the Mediterranean Sea each day- based on Coastal Municipalities Water Utility (CMWU) assessment in April this year.

Due to the impossibility of conducting adequate testing in Gaza due to Israeli restrictions, the analysis combined remote sensing with open-source data, analysis of likely causes, types and locations of contamination based on Israeli strikes and other incident data, and existing research of conflict-related contamination in other contexts including Iraq, Serbia, Lebanon and Ukraine.

The absence of a full, independent, field-based post-conflict environmental assessment is a direct consequence of Israel’s continued refusal of independent access to Gaza. Without sustained and unimpeded access for environmental experts, assessment teams and technical specialists, the field surveys required cannot be conducted. As a result, contamination cannot be fully characterised, monitored or mitigated, while civilians continue to be exposed to hazards which cannot be thoroughly examined.

Gaza has an estimated 61 million tonnes of rubble - approximately eight times the debris estimated in Mosul following the 2017 conflict, and three times the combined debris generated in Aleppo and Homs during the Syrian conflict. The rubble creates a vast environmental management challenge, with the potential for hazardous materials to be dispersed through dust, soil and water.

Long-term climate burden: Emissions across the wider conflict cycle, including reconstruction, are estimated at 33.2 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent - roughly equivalent to Palestine’s national emissions over almost six years at its 2023 level.

item.title: Peru: PER: Earthquake - 11-2026 - 6.7 Earthquake Junin (2026-11-21)
item.description:
Country: Peru
Sources: Cruz Roja Peruana, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Sources for data marked as Other

(1) COEN-INDECI, REPORTE-COMPLEMENTARIO N.° 16238 - Sismo de Magnitud 6.7 con Epicentro en Junín, 21 November 2026 (official situation report). (2) RPP Noticias. “Fuerte sismo en Junín: Indeci reporta ocho heridos y más de 120 viviendas afectadas en su más reciente balance” (21 November 2026): https://rpp.pe/peru/junin/fuerte-sismo-en-junin-indeci-reporta-ocho-heridos-y-mas-de-120-viviendas-afectadas-en-su-mas-reciente-balance-noticia-1718981 (3) Infobae Perú. “Sismo de 6.7 en Junín dejó 128 viviendas afectadas, 4 destruidas, 8 heridos y una universidad comprometida” (21 November 2026): https://www.infobae.com/peru/2026/11/21/sismo-de-67-en-junin-dejo-128-viviendas-afectadas-4-destruidas-8-heridos-y-una-universidad-comprometida/ Note. Estimated affected population (450 people) calculated from 128 affected households reported by INDECI using an average household size of 3.5 persons per household.

Description

On 20 November 2026 at 19:10 hrs local time, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck the Junín region of Peru, with impacts reported across Junín, Pasco and neighboring areas. According to the latest official COEN-INDECI report, issued on 21 November 2026 at 01:40 hrs, six people were reported injured, while no deaths or missing persons had been officially recorded at the time of publication. Initial assessments identified damage to housing, public infrastructure and basic services, including temporary power outages and road access restrictions caused by landslides and rockfalls. REPORTE COMPLEMENTARIO N.º 16249 - 21/11/2026 / COEN - INDECI / 08:20 HORAS (Reporte N.° 3) SISMO DE MAGNITUD 6.7 CON EPICENTRO EN EL DISTRITO DE JUNÍN - JUNÍN - INDECI Tarea de Todos

Subsequent updates communicated by INDECI and reported by national media indicate that the number of injured people increased to eight, with 128 houses affected and four houses destroyed. Damage was also reported to two churches, one hospital, one health centre and facilities of the Universidad Peruana Los Andes in Chanchamayo. Based on the reported number of affected households and applying an average household size of 3.5 persons, an estimated 450 people may have been affected by the earthquake. Damage and needs assessments remain ongoing, and figures may be revised as additional information becomes available.

At the time of reporting, all IFRC personnel present in the country have reported being safe, with no injuries or operational impacts affecting personnel confirmed.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: No

NS Requests International Assistance: No

Information Bulletin Published

No

Actions taken by others

Following the earthquake, the National Emergency Operations Center (COEN) and INDECI activated monitoring and coordination mechanisms to assess damages and support response actions in the affected areas. Local and regional authorities, together with sectoral institutions, continue conducting damage and needs assessments, while emergency response teams have been deployed to verify impacts on housing, health facilities, public infrastructure and road access. Authorities also reported ongoing efforts to restore access in areas affected by landslides and rockfalls and to coordinate assistance for affected households. According to statements by Luis Vásquez, Head of INDECI, emergency authorities continue to update impact figures and coordinate humanitarian assistance for affected families, including support for households whose homes were damaged or destroyed.

item.title: Argentina: ARG: Inundación - 11-2026 - Tormentas severas en San Francisco y General Cabrera (2026-11-21)
item.description:
Country: Argentina
Sources: Cruz Roja Argentina, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Fuentes para datos marcados como Otros

Desplazados (Otro): estimación de Cruz Roja Argentina sobre la base de "cerca de 80 familias" evacuadas en General Cabrera (Radio Villa María y Villa María Vivo, 20/11/2026), a razón de 4 personas por familia. No incluye General Deheza, que también registró evacuaciones sin cifra oficial. Heridos y muertos: sin casos reportados por el Gobierno de Córdoba ni por los municipios de San Francisco y Calchín Oeste. Afectados: Estimación de Cruz Roja en base a recorridas en terreno con voluntariado local.

Solicitar asistencia

Gobierno requiere asistencia internacional: No

SN requiere asistencia internacional: No

Boletín informativo publicado

No

Acciones tomadas por Sociedad nacional

General

  • Evaluación de daños y análisis de necesidades
  • Primeros auxilios
  • Otros

Resumen:
Cruz Roja Argentina mantiene vigente la Emergencia Categoría 1 nacional por el fenómeno El Niño desde el 04/11/2026. El 20/11, ante el pedido de apoyo de Protección Civil de San Francisco, la Filial San Francisco declaró la Emergencia Categoría 1 junto con la Sede Central. Se activaron el Equipo Nacional de Monitoreo (ENMO) para el seguimiento y el Equipo Nacional de Emergencias (ENE) para apoyo remoto. La Dirección Nacional de Respuesta a Emergencias validó las líneas de acción de la Filial, con condiciones de seguridad del voluntariado, coordinación con los organismos competentes y reportes operativos. La Filial San Francisco puso en apresto a su voluntariado para salir a terreno en coordinación con Protección Civil y el comité de crisis municipal, y la Filial Córdoba sigue la situación con su Equipo Local de Monitoreo y difunde medidas de autoprotección.

Acciones tomadas por Federación

Resumen: La Delegación en Argentina de la FICR mantiene una comunicación constante y permanente con la SN en el marco de las operaciones vigentes de Cruz Roja Argentina,

Medidas tomadas por otros

Gobierno de Córdoba: el gobernador ordenó movilizar recursos; las áreas de Gobierno y Desarrollo Social coordinan con los intendentes, con participación de Recursos Hídricos, Gestión de Riesgo, Protección Civil, bomberos y fuerzas de seguridad. Desarrollo Social envía ayuda económica y camiones con insumos y relevará daños para entregar materiales de reconstrucción, sobre todo para techos. EPEC desplegó 8 cuadrillas (unas 25 personas) en San Francisco y 2 en Calchín Oeste. Municipalidad de San Francisco: comité de crisis con Bomberos Voluntarios, Policía y Guardia Local para despejar árboles, limpiar calles, relevar daños y visitar a las familias con daños graves. General Cabrera: bombeo y limpieza de canales con maquinaria provincial; la Provincia evalúa declarar el estado de desastre. Bomberos Voluntarios de Carrilobo asisten en Calchín Oeste. Empresas privadas y la cooperativa eléctrica de Luque apoyan la limpieza y el restablecimiento del servicio. No hay presencia de agencias de Naciones Unidas.

item.title: Brazil: BRA: Drought - 11-2026 - BRA: Drought and Forest Fire (2026-11-20)
item.description:
Country: Brazil
Sources: Cruz Vermelha Brasileira, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Sources for data marked as Other

The information was collected directly from the Brazilian Government’s Integrated Disaster Information System

Description

The state of Para is facing an environmental and humanitarian emergency streaming from a combination of prolonged drought. reduced water availability and the spread of forest fires.

This situation has impacted native vegetation, conservation areas, indigenous territories and traditional communities, while also compromising economic activities and the basic living conditions of rural and riverin populations.

The severity of the scenario extends well beyond the areas directly consumed by the flames. The drought increases community vulnerability by limiting access to water for consumption, hygiene, livestock and agricultural production.

Simultaneously, smoke from the fires can exacerbate respiratory issues. hinder de movement of people and disrupt local services. In November 11th by the Decree 5767 the Federal Government declared a state of emergency in 61 municipalities across Para affected by forest fires. This declaration allows the municipal governments to request for federal support for emergency response and humanitarian assistance. In the Marajo region. the municipalities of Cachoeira do Arari and Soure require particular attention regarding the protection of rural areas and the stenghtening of local reponse capacities.

In Santarem the situation is particularly complex: the drought is compromising water supplies and river transport and livelihoods while fires are degradating air quality and threatening conservation areas creating a situation that must be addressed as environmental, public health and humanitarian crisis.

In Alter Do Chao, the gravity of the situation stems not only from fires within the APA but also within the Borari territory home the indigenous borari community (12000 people) that is organised in local brigades essential for a response that respect social, cultural and traditions.

From a humanitarian perspective, immediate priorities must include ensuring access to potable water and food security, providing healthcare, protecting traditional communities, and offering logistical support to response teams.

At the same time, it is necessary to strengthen prevention, oversight, and environmental restoration efforts to reduce the risk of future fires and prevent the emergency from persisting even after the flames have been brought under control.

Request For Assistance

Government Requests International Assistance: -

NS Requests International Assistance: Yes

Information Bulletin Published

Requested

Actions taken by National Society

General

  • Other
  • First Aid

Summary: Monitoring of the situation, fist aid and prevention campaigns

Actions taken by others

IBAMA / Prevfogo: Mobilization of firefighting brigades, direct fire suppression, environmental oversight, issuance of fines, imposition of land-use embargoes, and holding parties accountable for illegal burning. ICMBio – Combating fires in federal conservation units, mobilizing firefighting crews, aircraft, and vehicles, protecting traditional communities, and distributing water and supplies to affected families. Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change (MMA) – Coordination and alignment of environmental initiatives between federal and state governments, monitoring of risks, and integration of the institutions involved. Ministry of Integration and Regional Development (MIDR) / National Civil Defense – Recognition of emergency situations, analysis of work plans, and release of funds for humanitarian assistance and disaster response. National Public Security Force: Operational support for environmental teams and reinforcement of firefighting efforts in priority municipalities. Ministry of Justice and Public Security: Support for the mobilization of the National Public Security Force, and the provision of operational and aerial resources to the most affected regions. Ministry of Defense / Armed Forces: Institutional and logistical support for federal firefighting operations. Ministry of Agrarian Development and Family Farming (MDA): Support for vulnerable rural populations, including preventive food security measures and the early distribution of basic food baskets. Chief of Staff of the Presidency of the Republic: Interministerial coordination via the Situation Room for Forest Fire Control. Pará Military Fire Brigade (CBMPA): Direct firefighting, mobilization of specialized teams, coordination of operations, and protection of threatened communities. State Civil Defense Coordination (CEDEC-PA): Monitoring of climate-related risks, issuance of alerts, coordination of the state-level response, and liaison with municipal and federal civil defense agencies. State Secretariat for Environment, Climate, and Sustainability (Semas): Environmental monitoring, provision of equipment, and support for the organization of firefighting and prevention operations. Public Security Air Group (Graesp): Provision of helicopters for the transport of personnel, reconnaissance, and support for aerial operations. Pará Military Police (PMPA): Reinforcement of security and support for integrated firefighting operations. Civil Police / Specialized Environmental Agencies: Support for the investigation of arson and the identification of those responsible for illegal burning.

item.title: Zimbabwe - Drought Anticipatory Action | DREF Operation (MDRZW031)
item.description:
Country: Zimbabwe
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

11-09-2026

What happened, where and when?

Existing vulnerability and drought risk

Zimbabwe remains highly vulnerable to recurrent droughts driven by climate variability, El Niño events and the growing effects of climate change. Repeated drought episodes have increasingly affected agricultural production, food security, water availability, livestock health and household livelihoods, particularly in rural areas that depend heavily on rain-fed agriculture and natural resource-based livelihoods. Communities in drought-prone areas continue to face constrained coping capacities due to successive climate shocks, limited livelihood diversification and persistent economic challenges.

The impacts of the 2023/2024 El Niño-induced drought demonstrated the magnitude of these vulnerabilities. Reduced agricultural production, depletion of household food stocks, deterioration of water sources and declining livelihood opportunities contributed to widespread humanitarian needs across the country. The 2024 Zimbabwe Livelihoods Assessment Committee (ZimLAC) assessment estimated that approximately 5.9 million people were food insecure in rural areas, while access to basic water services declined significantly. Although these figures relate to the previous drought season, they highlight the scale of humanitarian impacts that can result from severe rainfall deficits and underscore the vulnerability of communities entering another potentially poor season.

Current food security and livelihood conditions indicate that many households have not fully recovered from previous shocks. According to the FEWS NET Food Security Outlook Update (August 2026-January 2027), poorer households in districts such as Chivi and Buhera had already exhausted own-produced food stocks earlier than normal and were increasingly dependent on market purchases. The April 2026 Second Round Crop, Livestock and Fisheries Assessment (CLAFA 2) similarly reported below-average agricultural production in several drought-prone districts. At the same time, elevated staple food prices, declining water availability, deteriorating pasture conditions and reduced livelihood opportunities continue to increase household vulnerability.

These underlying vulnerabilities are particularly pronounced in Chivi, Buhera, Mudzi, Mbire and Kariba districts, where many households are entering the 2026/27 agricultural season with limited food reserves, fragile livelihoods and reduced capacity to absorb further climate-related shocks.

Forecast evidence and anticipated drought risk

The operation is triggered by credible seasonal forecast information indicating an elevated likelihood of drought conditions during the 2026/27 rainfall season. The Meteorological Services Department (MSD), through the National Climate Outlook Forum (NACOF) held on 11 September 2026, forecast a high probability of below-normal rainfall across much of Zimbabwe between October 2026 and March 2027, associated with the development of a strong El Niño event and the potential influence of a positive Indian Ocean Dipole. These conditions are expected to increase the likelihood of delayed rainfall onset, prolonged dry spells, above-average temperatures and reduced soil moisture availability during critical stages of crop production.

This outlook is consistent with forecasts issued by the Thirty-Third Southern Africa Regional Climate Outlook Forum (SARCOF-33), which highlighted an elevated probability of below-normal rainfall and above-average temperatures across much of Southern Africa, including Zimbabwe. The convergence of national and regional forecasts indicates an increased risk of drought-related impacts on rain-fed agriculture, water resources, livestock production and rural livelihoods during the 2026/27 season.

Forecasts indicate that rainfall deficits during the October-December planting period could negatively affect planting decisions, crop establishment and germination, while continued moisture deficits during January-March could increase crop stress, reduce yields and worsen existing livelihood vulnerabilities. These projected conditions present a clear opportunity for anticipatory action before impacts materialize fully.

Anticipated humanitarian impacts

If forecast conditions materialize, vulnerable households are expected to experience further deterioration in food security, agricultural production and livelihood outcomes. Delayed rainfall, prolonged dry spells and above-normal temperatures may result in poor germination, reduced crop establishment, lower agricultural productivity and declining seasonal labour opportunities. Consequently, households may become increasingly dependent on markets at a time when purchasing power remains constrained.

Reduced rainfall and elevated temperatures are also likely to place additional pressure on water resources for domestic use, livestock and agricultural activities. Declining pasture availability, reduced livestock productivity and increased competition for limited water resources may further undermine household resilience and increase vulnerability among farming and agro-pastoral communities.

Without early intervention, affected households may increasingly resort to negative coping strategies such as reducing food consumption, selling productive assets, withdrawing children from school, distress livestock sales or accumulating unsustainable debt. These impacts are expected to be most severe among already vulnerable populations, including women-headed households, childheaded households, older persons, persons with disabilities, chronically ill individuals and extremely poor farming households.

Rationale for anticipatory action

The convergence of forecasted rainfall deficits, increasing climatic risk and pre-existing food security and livelihood vulnerabilities provides sufficient evidence to justify immediate anticipatory action. The forecast window provides a limited but critical opportunity to protect livelihoods before the most severe impacts of drought materialize. Delaying intervention until the effects of drought are fully observed would significantly reduce the effectiveness of agricultural support measures and increase the likelihood of humanitarian deterioration.

Through this DREF operation, the Zimbabwe Red Cross Society (ZRCS) will implement forecast-based anticipatory actions aimed at reducing the projected impacts of drought on vulnerable households. The operation will prioritize the timely distribution of droughttolerant and short-season crop varieties to 1,800 vulnerable farming households in Chivi, Buhera and Mudzi districts, combined with the dissemination of localized drought early warning information, climate adaptation messaging, water conservation measures and livestock protection advisories across Chivi, Buhera, Mudzi, Mbire and Kariba districts. These interventions are intended to support informed decision-making, protect agricultural production and strengthen household resilience before drought conditions worsen.

To complement implementation, ZRCS will concurrently conduct operational monitoring and assessment activities across the five targeted districts. These activities will support the monitoring of drought progression, identify emerging vulnerabilities, assess the effectiveness of anticipatory actions and strengthen evidence-based decision-making should conditions deteriorate beyond the forecast scenario. The assessments are therefore a supporting component of the operation and do not determine whether anticipatory actions are undertaken.

Implementation of planned early actions, particularly seed distribution within the critical planting window, will proceed independently of assessment activities.

The operation is therefore designed to act on available forecast information and existing vulnerability evidence now, while using concurrent monitoring and assessment to refine operational understanding, support accountability and inform any future preparedness or humanitarian response decisions that may become necessary should drought conditions worsen beyond anticipated levels.

item.title: Historic failure at COP31 is a devasting blow to children around the world – Save the Children
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

Children are extremely vulnerable to the impacts of the climate crisis, with an average of 330 million children per year experiencing severe climate disasters between January 2022 and September 2026—up nearly 50% in the previous five-year period.

ANTALYA, 22 NOVEMBER – Children have been dealt a devastating blow at COP31 today after countries failed to agree on a final deal that would deliver a meaningful response to the climate crisis, Save the Children said.

The inability of countries to reach agreement on issues such as transitioning away from fossil fuels and on providing the scale and quality of climate finance needed has left COP31 without a meaningful outcome. While backsliding was avoided, failure cannot be mistaken for progress, said Save the Children. At a time when children are already facing escalating climate impacts, this outcome signals that protecting their lives and futures remains secondary to preserving the systems and industries driving the crisis.

Children are extremely vulnerable to the impacts of the climate crisis, with an average of 330 million children per year experiencing severe climate disasters between January 2022 and September 2026—up nearly 50% in the previous five-year period.

Shruti Agarwal, Senior Climate Adviser, Save the Children UK, said:

"COP31 will be remembered as the conference where the world turned its back on climate ambition. Children are the ones most impacted by this failure; their lives and futures continue to be the ones to suffer.

"While decision makers spent days negotiating behind closed doors, they ultimately failed to reach an agreement, leaving children to bear the consequences of a climate crisis they did not create. Across the world, children are missing school, losing safe places to play, being forced from their homes and seeing their futures threatened by floods, wildfires, drought and extreme heat. The impacts may look different from one child to the next, but the reality is the same: no child should pay the price for a crisis they did not cause.

“Crucially this summit has failed to deliver the progress needed to transition away from fossil fuels or provide the scale and quality of climate finance that children and families urgently need.

"Every decision on addressing climate change shapes the world children will inherit, and today's failure to act will be felt for years to come. The progress made in recognising and advancing children's rights must not be allowed to unravel in future negotiations. Instead, it must serve as the foundation for greater ambition and urgent action.

"What happens next matters. Governments must return to the table next year ready to collaborate and determined to put children, especially those living on the front lines of the climate crisis, at the heart of the decisions that will define their future.”

ENDS

Peter is 14 years old and lives in Western Province in Zambia with his mother, Masiye (28), his brothers Munkobwe (2) and Mudla (12) and his sister Namasisku (7). Masiye farms maize, ground nuts and beans to provide for her children. The rainy season in Zambia normally stretches from October to March, but during the 2023/24 rainy season there have been intense dry spells and Masiye says they have gone days, weeks and months without rain. Her ground nut and bean crops have failed, and her maize crops – which were due to be harvested in May – have already shrivelled up and died. Masiye says they have cut back to two meals a day and that her children tell her constantly that they’re hungry. Masiye and her children have resorted to foraging for wild fruits and nuts – which are also in short supply due to the failed rains – but they have to be careful what parts of the fruits and nuts they eat as they can be toxic. There are also days when their borehole dries up and they have to dig a hole in the ground to get water. Peter says when he’s hungry he feels dizzy and can’t see properly, and this is impacting on his studies. He says sometimes he doesn’t go to school because he’s too hungry or because he must help his mother find food and water. Seven out of 10 provinces in Zambia have been impacted by the country’s worst drought in 20 years and the government has declared a national emergency. More than 1 million children are facing severe food shortages and hunger as the El Niño induced dry spell kills crops and dries up water sources. Sacha Myers / Save the Children

Since 2022, one in three children worldwide, or 911 million children, have been exposed to climate disasters.

12-year-old Jamer, lives in a small community called a “rancheria” in La Guajira on the northern tip of Colombia. He is part of the largest indigenous group in the country, the Wayuu tribe, and lives with his mother, stepfather and five siblings, the youngest is just a baby. The continuing drought and unpredictable seasons have hit his community hard. The once reliable rain patterns, guiding their crop cultivation, have shifted, leading to food shortages. The lack of water is taking its toll, especially on children. Jamer speaks of sickness and, sadly, cases where children have lost their lives due to water-related diseases. One of the main water sources they have available is the “Jaguey”, an open pool that relies on rainwater, several miles from his home that is also used by livestock. They often have to drink it despite the risks to their health. If the rain doesn’t arrive, there is a deep well close to their home, but that is saline, and dangerous for children. He’s exhausted by their daily hunt for fresh water in the blistering heat and worries for his younger brothers and sisters that they may go without. Other families in the community now pay for water to be trucked to their communities, but Jamers home is too remote and difficult for lorries to reach, so they must survive with what they have. Due to the years of drought when it does rain the rivers become impassable due to flooding, and the damage they have caused has created ravines in the landscape. He is concerned about what the impending impact of El Nino will be on his community, given the struggles they already face. But he still dreams of a better future for his community – one with access to clean water, quality education, and the ability to grow crops. Jamer is part of a Save the Childre program to promote resilience amongst the Wayuu community to the changing climate and promote traditional cultural practices. Strong quotes: "We are exhausted searching for water. The worst is that the easy one to find is the salty one, that's all." "The El Niño phenomenon is not convenient for us; it is better the La Niña phenomenon because it brings rain, if we want pure water because it is pure and comes from the sky." "The environment is also polluted when the garbage is burned, and the air is polluted, and the children are the ones who suffer from that." "We are very affected by the El Niño phenomenon because it has not rained, so the well is always contaminated." "Water is indispensable for our planting because it has not been raining lately." "Our crops die quickly; last time we planted beans, and they died as well as the corn because we poured the brackish (salty) water on them and left them." Angela Ponce / Save the Children

With climate disasters increasingly disrupting children's lives, education and futures, young people across the world are finding creative ways to influence decisions that will affect the planet they inherit.

item.title: Afghanistan: المفوضية ووكالة الإمارات للمساعدات توقعان اتفاقية بقيمة 3 مليون دولار أمريكي لدعم العائدين إلى أفغانستان | مفوضية اللاجئين
item.description:
Countries: Afghanistan, United Arab Emirates
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

وقعت المفوضية السامية للأمم المتحدة لشؤون اللاجئين ووكالة الإمارات للمساعدات الدولية اتفاقية بقيمة 3 مليون دولار أمريكي لدعم الإدماج وخدمات الحماية للعائدين الأفغان في كل من ولايات كابول، هرات وقندوز.

وقع الاتفاقية كل من أنطون لييس غارسيا، مساعد المفوض السامي لشؤون العمليات، وسعادة نصار المبارك، نائب رئيس وكالة الإمارات للمساعدات الدولية، على هامش معرض ومؤتمر إيديكس جنيف 2026.

جاء التوقيع بعد انعقاد اجتماع مائدة مستديرة رفيع المستوى دعت إليه وكالة الإمارات للمساعدات بالتعاون مع المفوضية، تحت عنوان "حلول الإسكان بعد النزوح: من المأوى الطارئ إلى التعافي والاندماج"، والتي شارك فيها مختصون من عدة منظمات تابعة للأمم المتحدة والمنظمات الإنسانية إلى جانب ممثلين من القطاع الخاص والمجتمعات المتأثرة بالنزوح.

بفضل المساهمة، ستقدم المفوضية المساكن الدائمة والقادرة على مواجهة التغير المناخي والمزودة بأنظمة الطاقة الشمسية ومرافق الصرف الصحي لنحو 422 أسرة أفغانية عائدة (ما يقرب من 2,950 شخصاً).

كما سيعزز المشروع خدمات الحماية للعائدين والأفراد الأكثر ضعفاً من المجتمعات المضيفة، مع التركيز على النساء والفتيات والأطفال. حيث سيتم استهداف ما يقرب من 3,950 امرأة وفتاة من خلال أنشطة دعم حماية المرأة ورفع الوعي. فيما سيستفيد أكثر من 1,200 طفل من خدمات حماية الطفل، بما في ذلك الدعم النفسي والاجتماعي، وإدارة الحالات، وبرامج التوعية المجتمعية.

قال سعادة الدكتور طارق أحمد العامري، رئيس مجلس إدارة وكالة الإمارات للمساعدات: "قد تسهم الخيمة في إنقاذ حياة إنسان، لكنها لا تستطيع إعادة بناء حياته. بالنسبة للأسر العائدة إلى أفغانستان، فإن الاتفاقية التي نوقعها اليوم بين وكالة الإمارات للمساعدات والمفوضية تعني تمكينها من امتلاك مسكن دائم يوفر لها الأمن والأمان والسلام، ويشكل نقطة انطلاق نحو مستقبل مزدهر. ونحن ندعو الحكومات والمنظمات الإنسانية وشركاء التنمية والمانحين إلى تضافر الجهود من أجل مساعدة الأسر حول العالم على خوض هذه الرحلة."

من جانبه، قال لييس غارسيا: "يعد الإسكان الآمن عنصراً أساسياً من عناصر الحماية وركيزة محورية في دعم الإدماج المستدام للعائدين. من خلال الشراكة مع وكالة الإمارات للمساعدات الدولية، نسعى إلى مساعدة الأسر الأفغانية العائدة على إعادة بناء حياتها بمزيد من الكرامة والأمان. وقد أكدت النقاشات التي شهدها اجتماع المائدة المستديرة اليوم على أهمية توسيع نطاق الوصول إلى حلول الإسكان المستدام الذي يتطلب عقد الشراكات المبتكرة والاستثمارات المستدامة لمساعدة الأشخاص النازحين على التعافي وتعزيز مشاركتهم الفاعلة في مجتمعاتهم."

منذ مطلع عام 2026، عاد أكثر من 1.3 مليون أفغاني إلى البلاد، فيما عاد أكثر من 6.5 مليون أفغاني خلال السنوات الثلاث الماضية منذ عام 2023. وتصنف الأسر العائدة ضمن الفئات الأكثر ضعفاً في أفغانستان. وفقاً لبيانات المفوضية، هناك أكثر من 90% من الأسر العائدة التي أفادت بأنها تعجز عن تلبية احتياجاتها الأساسية. كما تتسبب الأعداد الكبيرة من العائدين والوتيرة المتسارعة لعودتهم في فرض ضغوط هائلة على المجتمعات المحلية والخدمات والأسواق. تواصل المفوضية العمل مع أفغانستان وجيرانها من أجل تهيئة الظروف اللازمة للعودة الآمنة والطوعية والكريمة.

item.title: Yemen Market and Trade Bulletin October 2026 - Issued on 21st November 2026
item.description:
Country: Yemen
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

SHORT-TERM OUTLOOK AND IMPLICATIONS ON FOOD SECURITY:

While Yemen’s acute food security crisis—with roughly 18.7 million people (over half the population) facing acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or worse)—remains driven by heavy import dependency, rising food and fuel prices, severe humanitarian funding deficits, and climate and rainfall shocks, conditions have deteriorated sharply amid renewed frontline conflict and regional spillover effects. Since July 2026—and intensifying in September around Ta’iz, along the western coast, and across southern flashpoints—escalating hostilities and displacement have placed severe strain on overstretched services and existing displaced populations, while access constraints and road/maritime disruptions have slowed trade flows, pushed up freight and fuel costs, and restricted humanitarian reach. These compounding shocks—aggravated by funding shortfalls and climate stress—are eroding household purchasing power and driving acute deprivation, with millions facing IPC Phase 3 or worse conditions and localized emergency/catastrophe risks in late 2026.

KEY HIGHLIGHTS:

  • EXCHANGE RATES: Currency stability continued. The exchange rate remained broadly stable in GoY-controlled areas, trading 4% below its level a year earlier and 8% below the three-year average—indicating a firmer Yemeni rial against both benchmarks.
  • FOOD PRICES: Key staples became more expensive. In GoY-controlled areas, flour and basmati rice prices rose by 7.4% and 6.3% month-on-month, while sunflower oil and beans increased by 3.3% and 3.6%, respectively.
  • MINIMUM FOOD BASKET (MFB): Food-basket costs increased. Minimum Food Basket (MFB) costs in GoY-controlled areas rose 2% month-on-month from August, standing 7% above September 2025 levels and 2% above the three-year average—further squeezing household food affordability.
  • FOOD AND FUEL IMPORTS: Grain arrivals in GoY areas declined sharply. Recorded wheat and flour imports fell by 1.5% nationally and by 42.5% through southern ports. Recorded petrol and diesel imports also decreased by 9.9%; however, the absence of northern records limits the interpretation of this trend.
  • FUEL PRICES: Official diesel eased but remained elevated. Diesel prices fell by 4.5% month-on-month while petrol remained broadly stable; however, both fuels stayed substantially above last year's levels and their three-year averages.
  • TERMS OF TRADE (ToT): Flour purchasing power weakened. The Government of Yemen’s casual labor-to-flour terms of trade declined by 7.2% month-on-month and 23.1% year-on-year. Agricultural and composite livestock-to-flour ratios also decreased.
  • CASUAL LABOR WAGE RATES: Daily rates barely adjusted. In GoY-controlled areas, casual wages slipped 0.4% month-on-month and remained 9.7% below year-ago levels, while agricultural wages edged up by 0.4%.
  • LIVESTOCK PRICES: Modest recovery offered limited relief. Goat and local sheep prices increased month-on-month by 1.6% and 2.4%, respectively, but remained below their levels from the previous year.

item.title: DR Congo: Evaluation conjointe des besoins en matière d’Education et Protection RDC-2026
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Sources: Education Cluster, Save the Children, UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Le rapport de l’évaluation conjointe des besoins d’Education et de Protection menée en collaboration avec le secteur de la Protection met en évidence les résultats suivants :

  • Taux d’abandon de 12,5 % au cours de l’année scolaire 2025-2026, principalement lié aux difficultés socio-économiques des ménages, aux déplacements forcés, aux travaux domestiques, ainsi qu’aux mariages et grossesses précoces.
  • 131 établissements sur 266 (50 %) rapportent des absences scolaires liées à la gestion des menstruations.
  • 76 responsables d’établissements sur 266 (28%) affirment que les établissements ont subi des pillages ou vols perpétrés par des groupes armés depuis le début de l’année 2026, tandis que 47 sur 266 (18%) ont relevé l’occupation de salles de classe par des forces ou groupes armés.
  • L’inclusion des enfants en situation de handicap demeure limitée, avec peu de mesures spécifiques favorisant leur participation et leur maintien à l’école.
  • Seuls 51 établissements sur 266 (19 %) disposent d’un accès à l’eau potable provenant de leur principale source d’approvisionnement.
  • 114 établissements (43 %) ne disposent pas de latrines séparées pour les filles et les garçons.
  • 101 établissements sur 266 (38 %) signalent la présence d’enfants présentant des signes de détresse psychosociale, notamment des cauchemars, une tristesse persistante, une anxiété élevée, de la fatigue extrême, des comportements violents ou de l’isolement.
  • Seuls 70 établissements sur 266 (26%) disposent d’un mécanisme de référencement VBG adapté aux enfants et permettant l’orientation vers des services spécialisés.

Malgré ces défis, les consultations avec les enfants montrent que l’école reste perçue comme un espace de protection, de stabilité et d’espoir. Comme l’a souligné un enfant de 8 à 11 ans : « A l’école, on étudie et on oublie la guerre. »
